newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt faces opposition over economic strategy.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt faces opposition over economic strategy.

text.p: Italy's government is expected to unveil its rolling three-year economic strategy this week in the face of opposition from trades union leaders and hard-left allies to cutting pensions and welfare payments.

The strategy, known as the economic and financial planning document (DPEF), is due to be approved by the cabinet on Friday and will outline how the government intends to cut another 25 trillion lire ($15 billion) from the public deficit in next year's budget.
The DPEF is a crucial part of Italy's plans for stabilising state finances and keeping alive hopes of joining a European currency union by the planned 1999 start date.

Foreign Trade Minister Augusto Fantozzi said on Friday that although the government had agreed on the size of budget it was still debating what the exact mix should be between spending cuts and fresh revenue-raising measures.

Italian newspapers have reported that the government plans to reduce spending by 17 trillion lire -- including eight trillion lire in social security and welfare spending cuts -- and to raise eight trillion lire in increased revenues.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who holds talks with key political allies in his centre-left coalition on Monday, is expected to spell out details of the strategy to union leaders when he meets them on Thursday.

Sergio D'Antoni, leader of the CISL trade union confederation, signalled at the weekend that Prodi can expect a rough ride if the government sticks to its reported plan to pare welfare spending by eight trillion lire in the 1998 budget.
"I think it is difficult to carry out a reform of the welfare state by cutting eight trillion lire," D'Antoni told his union congress on Saturday.

D'Antoni has also criticised government plans to raise more revenue by widening value added tax (VAT) bands on the grounds that such a move would fuel inflation and "hit popular consumption, affecting prices of bread, pasta and milk".
But the loudest opposition to cuts in social spending comes from Fausto Bertinotti, leader of the hard-left Communist Refoundation Party.
The government depends for its survival in the lower house of parliament on support from Communist Refoundation.
Bertinotti has said he accepts the idea of shaking up an outmoded welfare state but opposes wholesale cuts.
"We believe that reforms must be carried out to the welfare state, which no longer corresponds to people's fundamental needs. But this must be done without cuts or taxes," he said.
Government attention has focused on so-called length of service pensions, which in some civil service jobs can be drawn after paying as little as 30 years of contributions into a state pensions plan.

Nobel prize-winning economist Franco Modigliani has said that Bertinotti has no right to take part in the debate on pensions reform because his wife Gabriella, who works in local government, has herself lodged an application to retire early.
One of Prodi's closest economic advisers, Paolo Onofri, said in a newspaper interview on Sunday that Italy would pay dearly if it failed to get to grips with welfare reforms in the next few months.
He told Corriere della Sera that the government's three-year economic programme aimed to prevent social spending from spinning out of control rather than to impose swingeing cuts.
"There are still three or four months left to get our hands on the reform of the welfare state and to make a structural impact on spending," said Onofri.
"The cost of failing to act would be enormous. Exclusion from Europe, high interest rates, recession, even the risk of a financial crisis," he added.
